markers.title: Restaurants reporting, not reports filed
markers.finding: An area safety lead received an automated reminder email listing how many incident and hazard reports each restaurant had made, period to date and year to date, and used it to follow up.
markers.decision: The first tile counts restaurants that reported, not reports received, and names how many have been silent for a fortnight. The number an area manager acts on is how many teams have gone quiet.
markers.rejected: A total report count for the area, which rises when one busy restaurant reports a lot and hides eleven others.

markers.title: Overdue actions named by restaurant
markers.finding: Reviewing weekly, an area safety lead found many incidents in their area sitting overdue, and a backlog creates pressure to close reports quickly without the proper steps.
markers.decision: The overdue tile breaks the number down by restaurant on the tile itself, so the follow-up is a named conversation rather than a queue to clear.
markers.rejected: A single overdue count linking to a mixed list, which invites bulk closing rather than a conversation with the three managers who own the work.

markers.title: The quiet restaurants sort to the top
markers.finding: Zero reports in a period was already treated as a signal to check in, not as good news.
markers.decision: The table opens sorted so the three restaurants that have gone quiet sit first, tinted, with a dot on the name. The rule the area safety lead already applied is built into the default view.
markers.rejected: Sorting by report volume, which puts the restaurants that need attention at the bottom of a twelve-row table.

markers.title: Hazards per incident as the leading indicator
markers.finding: Some restaurant groups run competitions and recognition for reporters and report more. The research cautioned that rewarding counts encourages low-value reports, and suggested recognising outcomes instead.
markers.decision: The ratio of hazards to incidents is the headline measure, tinted healthy, watch or low. Many hazards and few incidents means a team finding problems before they hurt someone, which volume alone cannot show.
markers.rejected: A leaderboard of top reporters, which rewards volume over value and was flagged in the research as a risk.

markers.title: Days since the last report, not a tick
markers.finding: Because reports arrive verbally, the manager decides what is worth logging, checks the story and enters it. Reporting is strong where the manager has built the routine and weak where they have not.
markers.decision: Time since the last report is shown as a badge that ages, so a manager routine that has lapsed shows up within a fortnight rather than at the period review.
markers.rejected: A compliant or non-compliant flag, which cannot distinguish a restaurant that reported yesterday from one that reported six days ago.

markers.title: The row ends in a conversation
markers.finding: Location did not predict safety culture. The manager did. Where a manager had built a reporting culture, reporting was strong regardless of the suburb, which moved the recommendations towards manager routines.
markers.decision: Only the flagged rows carry an action, and the action is Talk this week, addressed to the named manager. The finding that the manager is the variable is what the row asks the area manager to act on.
markers.rejected: A Send reminder button on every row, which is the email the research found told no one anything.

markers.title: One panel per restaurant, one shared scale
markers.finding: The reminder email listed period-to-date counts per restaurant. Counts alone could not say whether a low number meant a safe restaurant or a silent one.
markers.decision: Twelve panels on the same zero-to-eight scale show the shape of reporting over eight weeks. A line that fades to the axis reads as a routine that stopped, which a single period count cannot show.
markers.rejected: One combined chart with twelve series, which becomes unreadable and hides the restaurants that flatten out.

markers.title: The measure explains itself on the screen
markers.finding: Team members and managers had no shared definition of a reportable incident, and nobody had told them where the threshold sat.
markers.decision: The card next to the data says in three lines why many hazards is a good sign, why silence is a question rather than a result, and what the ratio replaces. A new area manager can read the measure without training.
markers.rejected: A tooltip or a definitions page, which puts the reasoning somewhere nobody opens during a weekly review.
